# On the Strangeness of Everyday Rituals

I've been thinking about how we perform the same small actions every morning without questioning them—brushing teeth, brewing coffee, checking our phones—and how bizarre this would seem to someone from another era. We're ritualists pretending to be practical.

The coffee ritual especially fascinates me. I don't think most people drink coffee because they're actually that tired. There's something else: the warm mug in cold hands, the smell, the three minutes of permission to stand still before the day demands things. It's a small ceremony disguised as caffeine delivery.

This makes me wonder what future generations will find strange about us. Probably the phone thing. The way we compulsively check these glowing rectangles even when we know nothing interesting happened in the last seven minutes. An archaeologist might conclude we were anxious creatures, constantly seeking reassurance from our devices.

But maybe that's not wrong. Maybe rituals aren't just about what they accomplish—they're about marking time, creating tiny anchors of meaning. A morning routine is a conversation with yourself about who you are. Coffee says: *I'm someone who takes a moment. I'm not rushing yet.*

The real strangeness isn't that we have rituals. It's that we pretend we don't. We dress them up in practicality: this is efficient, necessary, just how things are done. But humans have always needed ceremony. We've just become embarrassed about admitting it.

So I'll keep brewing my coffee, fully aware of the ritual. At least I'm honest about it.
